content_html:
For generations, anthropologists have treated the human habit of pet-keeping as a completely unique, highly anomalous cultural quirk. Why would an organism expend precious metabolic energy, share hard-won food reserves, and dedicate hours of labor to care for an entirely different species that offers zero genetic payout? The question has lingered at the edges of evolutionary biology for decades, largely unanswered because the evidence simply was not there. A landmark international review published in the journal Primates, led by Dr. Cyril Grueter of the University of Oxford, has changed that. The answer, it turns out, is that we are not nearly as unique as we thought.

The Grueter Database | 427 Cases Across 88 Primate Species

The research team drew data from a meticulous combination of peer-reviewed scientific literature, field observations from practicing primatologists, and verified media documentations spanning decades of fieldwork across Asia, Africa, and South America. The resulting database is the most comprehensive catalog of interspecific primate social behavior ever assembled: 427 distinct cases involving 88 different primate species and 127 partner species. Critically, 55 of those partner species were entirely non-primate animals, including domestic dogs, wild deer, forest pigs, grizzled squirrels, and even small rodents.

What makes the dataset especially powerful is its breadth across the primate order. The behaviors were documented in prosimians, New World monkeys, Old World monkeys, and apes, spanning the full phylogenetic range. This is not a quirk of one weird troop in one forest. It is a pattern distributed across the entire primate lineage, suggesting an ancient, deeply conserved capacity rather than a recent, culturally transmitted oddity.

The Spectrum of Primate Friendships | From Play to Adoption

The study reveals that primate interactions with other animals span a remarkably broad behavioral spectrum, mirroring the exact way human-animal bonds evolve across a human lifespan. Juvenile primates engage in high-intensity cross-species play, chasing, wrestling, and mock-fighting with animals they have no evolutionary reason to interact with. As primates age, these playful interactions transition into more deliberate affiliative behaviors: tactile grooming, carrying, and protective vigilance. At the rarest and most extraordinary peak of the spectrum lies full interspecific adoption, where a primate takes on long-term caretaking responsibility for an animal of an entirely different species.

The database documents an array of strikingly distinct pairings across the globe. In Thailand, wild stump-tailed macaques regularly seek out domestic dogs wandering near Buddhist temples, spending hours fastidiously picking dirt and parasites out of the dogs' fur in a grooming behavior indistinguishable from how they treat their own troop members. In Sri Lanka, tufted gray langurs have been documented gently stroking the backs of giant grizzled squirrels resting on tree branches, a behavior that serves no obvious survival function and appears to be purely affiliative. In the dense mountain forests of China, juvenile black-and-white snub-nosed monkeys frequently drop down from the canopy to engage in elaborate games of tag and mock-wrestling with wild and domestic pigs. At the Shanghai Zoo, researchers monitored a female northern white-cheeked gibbon that carried a small wild mouse in her palm for days, protecting it from other primates and treating it with immense physical gentleness.

The Case of Fortunata | A Marmoset Raised by Capuchins

The most extraordinary case highlighted in the review takes place in the woodlands of Brazil, detailing a phenomenon that looks remarkably like true human pet-keeping or adoption. In 2004, field biologists monitoring a troop of wild bearded capuchin monkeys noticed an adult female named Chiquinha carrying an infant on her back. The baby was not a capuchin. It was a marmoset, a drastically smaller, completely distinct monkey species from an entirely different primate family. The researchers named the tiny infant Fortunata.

What followed over the subsequent year shocked the scientific community. Chiquinha, and later a second female named Dende, raised Fortunata with the exact same level of hyper-vigilant maternal care given to biological capuchin infants. The entire troop adapted its social dynamic to accommodate their tiny companion. When young capuchins played with Fortunata, they consciously modified their physical strength to avoid injuring the fragile marmoset, a level of motor awareness and social consideration that is difficult to explain through standard behavioral models. Fortunata learned to understand capuchin vocalizations, foraged alongside the troop, and even actively participated in defensive maneuvers, helping the monkeys mob predatory snakes. She lived successfully as a member of the capuchin troop for over a year until reaching near-adulthood, a developmental span that represents an enormous investment of energy and protection from her adoptive family with zero genetic return.

Evolutionary Spillover | Why the Primate Brain Reaches Across Species

From a strict evolutionary perspective, behavior that does not advance your own genetic line is costly. Time spent grooming a dog is time not spent foraging, mating, or watching for predators. Food shared with an unrelated marmoset is calories not invested in your own offspring. Why, then, do primates possess such a remarkable capacity for cross-species empathy and socialization?

Dr. Grueter's team points to a phenomenon known as evolutionary spillover. Primates are hyper-social, highly cooperative animals that have evolved intense neural wiring optimized for empathy, maternal care, and play. These traits provide massive survival benefits when directed toward members of their own troop. Kin-directed grooming reinforces alliances. Maternal vigilance keeps infants alive. Juvenile play develops motor skills and social cognition essential for adult life. However, because the primate brain is incredibly curious and socially flexible, these deeply ingrained caretaking and playful impulses can easily spill over onto entirely different species that happen to trigger the same protective or social instincts.

The mechanism is not anthropomorphism. It is neural economy. A brain that evolved to say “small thing moving near me, protect it” or “friendly face, groom it” does not always check the species ID before acting. The behavioral machinery of social bonding is sufficiently general-purpose that it activates on dogs, squirrels, pigs, and marmosets just as readily as on fellow troop members, provided the triggering cues are present. As Dr. Grueter noted in a press release covered by Phys.org, these behaviors may not amount to pet-keeping exactly as humans know it, but they represent the fundamental evolutionary building blocks from which human-animal companionship eventually emerged.

What This Changes | Pet-Keeping Is Not a Human Invention

The Grueter study does not claim that monkeys keep pets in the human sense. A stump-tailed macaque grooming a temple dog is not filling out adoption paperwork or buying a leash. But the study fundamentally reframes the origin story of human-animal companionship. Pet-keeping has long been treated by anthropology as a cultural invention, a byproduct of domestication and settled civilization with no deeper biological roots. The Grueter database shows that the raw behavioral ingredients, cross-species play, grooming, protection, and adoption, exist across the primate order in wild, undomesticated populations. These are not learned behaviors transmitted through human culture. They are spontaneous expressions of primate social cognition operating in its default mode.

The implication is significant: when a human sits on a couch stroking a cat, or bends down to greet a dog at the park, they are not engaging in an isolated cultural habit invented by civilization. They are participating in an ancient behavioral tradition that traces back through millions of years of primate evolution, a tradition of curiosity, cross-species tolerance, and radical empathy that long predates the emergence of Homo sapiens. The urge to reach across the species divide and share space with another creature is one of the oldest, most natural impulses in the primate repertoire.
